utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 3rd of March, 2010. Let me first greet General Petkovic, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Coric, and Mr. Pusic. Good morning to the Defence counsel, to you, Mr. Scott, and all your team members, and a very good morning to all the people assisting us. Before we start, one first thing. Mr. Kovacic has to be on the transcript. Mr. Praljak is absent, therefore, you are assisting and representing him; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, thank you for asking. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now been recorded. General Petkovic, in a few moments you are going to answer questions by Mr. Scott. He's going to start with his cross-examination. You have attended many such occasions, many cross-examinations, and you know that Mr. Scott is going to ask you leading questions that may not please you, in which case you have to remain calm and cool-headed. You have to ponder the question he's putting to you, and you answer calmly. As was said on several occasions, cross-examination is a practice in which you answer, Yes, or, No, I don't know, I don't understand the question. And then should the Prosecutor wish to dig a little deeper, he will do so. But let's not go into long speeches, because the Prosecutor's time is precious and he has to put his case to you through the questions he's asking. Furthermore, I do invite the Defence counsel not to interrupt at any moment, because the Prosecutor does his job, even if you don't like it at times, that's what he does. And if you have objections, they must be on account of technical substantial errors, or technical issues, but not on the merits, because the Prosecutor is entitled to put his case through the questions he's going to ask Mr. Petkovic. Mr. Scott hardly ever intervened during your examination-in-chiefs and the cross-examination, so I hope you will do the same. What is important is the question and the answer. When I hear a question and I see that somebody's on his feet on the other side, I think that the answer that is about to be given is not going to have the same weight as if the answer had been provided without intervention of Defence counsel, or of counsel. So I think you get my drift. Mr. Petkovic, you've got the binders in front of you, so you can follow the documents as they are submitted to you. So very well. Everything's ready. General Petkovic has got his documents, and you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to each of Your Honours. Good morning to counsel, all those in and around the courtroom who are helping us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me, just as a housekeeping matter, indicate that, while, ultimately there are a number of binders of documents that might be used in the course of this examination. To make it easier, I hope, for everyone today, I believe all the exhibits -- the documents today will be in the first binder, with the exception that there might be a couple -- I think there are a couple of loose exhibits that, because of my fault, didn't make it into the binder. But we should in binder number 1, and I think in the course of the day there will be maybe a couple of loose exhibits as well. And in the days ahead, we'll probably move into some of the other binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petkovic, we know by now that you previously testified in both the Blaskic and Kordic cases under oath; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the Kordic case, where you testified the second time, that is, after the Blaskic testimony, at transcript page 26800, 26800, you affirmed and adopted your Blaskic testimony. You said: "There is nothing I have to change or would want to change." And is that still correct today? Do you stand by your Blaskic testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I stand by what I said in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, likewise, Mr. Petkovic, I am sure -- or at least I presume that in the course of preparing to give your testimony in this case, before you got up and Ms. Alaburic started putting questions to you, you had occasion to review your testimony in the Kordic case, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I went through my testimony in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask you, sir, a similar question as I asked you about your Blaskic testimony? Do you affirm your Kordic testimony as true and accurate, or is there anything in your Kordic testimony that you wish to change?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the testimony that I gave in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, we understand, I think, fairly well by now, sir, that you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina to take up certain of these new duties and responsibilities on about the 14th of April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's the date that I always refer to when speaking about the time at which I arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the 14th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, you've seen -- you've been sitting in this courtroom with all of us these past several years, and, of course, you've seen a number of the -- well, virtually all of the witnesses, I suppose, and seen a lot of documents. And there's just names of a few persons I'd like to cover with you, if you will, for a few moments. You saw Mr. Filipovic, who was here and testified in your case, and we also have some documents that we've seen a number of times from -- regarding Mr. Siljeg. You knew and know both those individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I know Colonel Filipovic, and I also know Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do I correctly assume, sir, that you brought Mr. Filipovic as a witness here because you believe that he was a good officer, a professional soldier, reliable and credible?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I hadn't believed that he was such a person, I certainly wouldn't have called him here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's what I thought. And you would trust his judgement? You respected his work in the past as a professional officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was at the head of the Main Staff, as far as I knew, there was nothing I could object to the duties performed by Colonel Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Siljeg, he was one of your senior officers from the very beginning, the documentation seems to show, from about the same time that you arrived. He took over very quickly as head of the -- or the commander of the North-West Operative Zone for most of the time, at least, relevant to this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Colonel Siljeg was there for a long time. When I arrived, he was already in the area. Later, he was the commander of the North-Western Herzegovina Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, the answer to my question would be, Yes. As you know already, time is precious. So you've repeated back to me the question I put to you, essentially the same information, but I do appreciate that you have confirmed Mr. Siljeg's role at the time. Mr. Siljeg was another JNA -- former JNA professional officer, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And like Mr. Filipovic, you found him to be a good, professional, and reliable officer, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Each in his own specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I must tell you that in the probably thousands, if not tens of thousands of documents that I've seen over the past few years including those in communications between you and Mr. Siljeg, I have never seen any complaints or criticisms that you directed towards Mr. Siljeg or his conduct during 1992/1993. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to remember these things now, but there probably wasn't any criticism. There were probably just certain requests that were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your Kordic testimony, you described the time when you arrived in Bosnia in mid-April, as we discussed a moment ago. You described it and used the words "it was an embryonic time in the establishment of the HVO armed forces"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you likewise testified in Kordic that prior to your arrival, there had been no one there to prepare and organise the HVO military; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the level that I later occupied, but at other levels in municipalities, yes, there were people who were responsible for organising the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said in Kordic, at 26691: "There was no one at the time to prepare and organise the Croatian Defence Council"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that what I had in mind was higher levels, not levels below the Main Staff in the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you heard Mr. Filipovic testify here, and Mr. Filipovic testified that when he came into the situation, he found the situation chaotic and almost nothing functioned properly. You would agree with that assessment, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully. It was the beginning. I don't really want to say that it had to be that way, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I don't think we need to pause and stop and look at it, in the interests of time, given your testimony, but I'll just mention, in fact, you gave an interview on the 31st of December, 1994, which, if the courtroom does wish to look at it, is P11167. And in that interview, you said then, many years ago, 15 years ago almost, what you said just now: "The Croatian Defence Council was neither organised nor structured. They lacked officers at the command level"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you saw your responsibility, on arriving on the scene as a former professional JNA officer -- you remained a professional officer, I suppose, but not in the JNA any longer. You said, about as your primary responsibility or activity, is organising the HVO as a military force; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to carrying out ongoing combat, the task was also to organise the HVO in a more efficient manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the operative zones or what became the operative zones, for example, Mr. Blaskic had been appointed commander or head of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone by late June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In June 1992, he was appointed as the commander of -- what was it officially called? Well, yes, we can say it was Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And by the fall of 1992, sir, these forms of organisations that had existed previously, and I think you may have mentioned it a moment or two ago, the municipal staffs, so the crisis staffs, by the fall of 1992 you had been successful in largely abolishing those, with a new structure based on brigades being put in place; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that came to an end towards the end of the year. We started doing this in the autumn, and it came to an end towards the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, there may have been different stages in different places, I agree, sir. But as early as September, you were giving orders to Mr. Blaskic, for example, as part of this new structure, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, but not all the units of the Municipal Staff had been transformed into brigades. This was the case in 1993. At the end of 1992, as far as I can remember, we had moved on to a brigade structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Then can we agree to this much and then move forward: And you I might not agree on an exact date, but you would agree, and we do seem to agree, that by late 1992, the brigade -- the HVO brigade structure was in place and going forward; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, at the end of 1992, and that's the system that was in place in 1993. So in 1992, as far as I can remember, these municipal staffs were completely dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during this same period of time, sir, the new BiH government forces, initially called the Territorial Defence, not the old Territorial Defence under the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but under the new Territorial Defence established by the BiH Presidency on the 8th of April, 1992, and then later became known as the ABiH or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, during this period that armed force was also being established and organised, April, May, June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And in June, I think that was when they went through the last stage. It went through several stages. I think it was in June that the official term for all the forces was the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And during this time, the BiH -- these BiH forces - let's just call them that for the moment - TO, ABiH, but they were essentially doing many of the same things, they were trying to get organised, they were looking for -- they were recruiting a number of former JNA officers, they were really doing a lot of the same things that the HVO -- that you were doing on the HVO side; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The procedure had to be identical because everything had to be done from the very beginning on both sides. No one was in a position to just come across units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic testified in the Kordic case, and I believe again here, that on the ABiH side, during this period April to July 1992 or so, there were actually more former JNA officers on the ABiH side, if you will, than in the HVO. Would you agree with him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, I fully agree, because most of the Muslims in the JNA were from the territory of the then Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Filipovic also testified that by June 1992, the Territorial Defence or the ABiH had developed actually into a much larger force, at least in terms of personnel and manpower, than the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The territory where it was being established was also larger and its population was larger. When I refer to "territory," I'm referring to the territory of Eastern Bosnia that was covered by units of the ABiH. There were no HVO members there, apart from in the Tuzla area. So the ABiH covered the entire territory of Eastern Bosnia. Bihac was also included.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness mentioned another town. The interpreter didn't hear the name. Could the witness please be asked to speak up, as he's speaking very softly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I think you will have heard that the interpreters would appreciate if you could speak a bit more loudly, please. Mr. Filipovic also said, sir, that as of the June 1992, the ABiH carried its part of the burden and responsibility and was on an equal footing in its ability to fight at the defence lines obviously against the Serbs. You also agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with that. Once it was formed, they took up certain positions, they were responsible for certain lines, and they were more or less capable of defending themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you turn, please, in the binder to P11219, P11219. It's loose, it's one of the loose ones, Your Honours, and the courtroom. I think it's right next to you there, sir. I can see it. P11219. Just very briefly, sir, this is a copy of a decision of the BiH Presidency, I believe, on the 18th of August, 1992, where they also were going through various organisation and reorganisation, and it was around this time that they went to -- just as you went to your structures, they went to a structure involving corps, correct, essentially regional corps?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, sorry, but at least myself, I haven't found it. Binder 1, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's loose, Your Honour. It's one of the loose exhibits. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in particular, sir, the fourth -- I'm going to direct your attention and the courtroom's attention to, under Article 1, Roman numeral I: "The 4th Corps, Mostar," and you see that. And if you turn over, I don't know about in the Croatian language version, but in the English version, below the second -- below the middle of the second page, and I'm sure you'll be able to find it, the area covered by the 4th Corps is described, and it says: "The 4th Corps, the headquarters of which is in Mostar." And then it covers these following areas: Bjelica, Capljina, Citluk, Gacko, Grude, Jablanica, Konjic, Ljubuski, Mostar, et cetera. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that the 4th Corps covered not all, not all, but much of the territory or municipalities claimed to comprise the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I should say something about the date. The 4th Corps was formed at the beginning of November 1992. On paper, it covered this area, but in no other way. So on paper, yes, it had these municipalities, but none of its forces were present in those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, there was a Muslim formation in the Mostar region, wasn't there, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can mention which municipalities these are. I think that would be fair, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well -- no, let me just focus on Mostar, for example. There was -- wasn't there something called the Independent Battalion, or the Mostar Brigade, or Mostar Battalion, that was primarily a Muslim unit, if you will, or ABiH unit?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That was the 1st Mostar Brigade at the time, which had been established some 20 days ago. It started -- establishment started in July 1992. All these other places, except for Jablanica and Konjic, were places where there was no one soldier of the ABiH to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if we have time, we'll come back to some of that eventually, perhaps. But we have the 4th Corps established, and we see the area which it was at least intended to cover. Now, we can stop briefly, perhaps, and this will be in the binder, on 4D00830. I think it's the last document in the first binder that we're using today, 4D00830. While you're looking for that, sir, just for the record, I'll say that this is your report on the work of the HVO, essentially from the time you arrived, it says on page 1 -- the report itself -- let me back up and say the report, itself, is dated February 4th, 1993, covering the period April 14, 1992, through December 31, 1992. And I think, sir, if you look through that, and we're not going to stop and look at the document in detail at all, but simply for you to know and for the courtroom to see that many of the things we've talked about in the last few minutes are, in fact, covered in your report. You talk about the organisation of the brigades. Under the second heading overall, not number 2, but at the end of, I guess, end of unit 1, you say: "General conclusion. Nowadays, HVO forces successfully hold under their control 90 per cent of the area mapped out as HZ-HB, and they are capable and ready to defend it, provide they get better material support." Item number 3: "Organisation of HVO forces. HVO forces were organised in the course of combat activities throughout the entire territory of HZ-HB. Organisation of HVO forces through temporary formations is almost finished, and nowadays we have the following scheme:" And then you lay out that scheme, basically, the HVO General or Main Staff for operational zones and the brigade structure in each of the zones. And we're going to come to that in just a few minutes. At the last item before number item 4, if you can find that, there's a section titled "4" that says "Personnel Issues and Drafting." We can use that, please, as a landmark, and if we look immediately above that, you say in your report: "Formation of brigades cancelled municipal staffs, and this added to commanding quality while units gained mobility"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated here, that by this means and at that moment, a small step toward a better organisation had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't such a small step, was it, sir? It was a rather large step, and largely you're responsible for it, to your credit. You had achieved, in a relatively short time, improving the HVO military organisation rather substantially. I don't think you have to be unduly modest in this situation. You did that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did that, but this couldn't have been a step of five miles. These were only the first steps. Like this, we let the municipalities know that they were not supposed to interfere, but to keep out of that. But certainly the fact that at least on paper we took away the extensive powers that the municipalities had had before was certainly a step forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you would agree, sir, again, with the view expressed by Mr. Filipovic, that: "By the end of 1992, the HVO was fairly organised and represented a significant fighting force"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO had its organisational structure on paper. Our assessment was that we had up to 45.000 men, and that was the utmost that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina could rally, not more than that, because simply there weren't enough Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With that background and that foundation laid, let's look, please, at Exhibit P11123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, one small question. As regards the last document, the 4D0830, do you intend to refer to Prozor again in future, because this document provides an explanation for the events in Prozor. If you get back to it, I will not put a question, but if you don't, I would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd have to say the honest answer to your question is, given the time constraints and the evolving nature of the cross and how time goes, I don't know for sure that we'll come back to it. So if you would like to ask your question, of course, I invite you to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, this is an extremely short question I'd like to put to you. I discover in this document, in paragraph 5, you explain the events in Prozor, and I read what you have written, that the Muslims attacked in Prozor, they attacked, in fact, because they wanted to take control of the hydroelectric power-plant. This is what you have written. Can you confirm this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can confirm that, Your Honour. I confirm everything I wrote here under item 5, and that refers to the Prozor region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that in Prozor, it was the Muslims who attacked, because they killed one of your soldiers. This is what you write. And the purpose was to control the hydroelectric power-plant. You explain that the HVO intervened and that extremist -- Muslim extremist groups were still provocative and fueling the conflict. It's always interesting to look at the document. And you add all of this for the benefit of KOS. What did you mean by this; that the Serbs were behind all of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, when I say "KOS," I must add that KOS wasn't manned by Serbs only. There were Croats, Slovenians, Muslims, Macedonians in their ranks too, everybody who had been citizens of Yugoslavia. So KOS wasn't manned only by ethnic Serbs. They may have been the majority because they were the most numerous group, but KOS comprised persons from all peoples, and whoever want to do join KOS would do so, irrespective of their ethnic affiliation. Or, rather, only those would be allowed to join who had been assessed by the KOS as being able to provide good quality work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the floor is yours again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could then turn, please, if you haven't done so already, to P11123, P11123, in, again, the first binder or the binder we're using today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a chart that I think it's come up before, and I mean to spend a lot of time on it, but I did want to touch on it in leading to something else. This was a chart that you prepared and was prepared and used by you in connection with your Blaskic testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that you again stand by this diagram or chart, if you will, as continuing to be true and accurate, according to you. Page 3 of the e-court. Yes, thank you. You stand by it, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I stand by this schematic I drew back then or, rather, which I drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I might just say for the record, sir, because we'll, again, not have time to cover everything that we might otherwise, but I think we're probably pretty much in agreement on most of the chart, you and I. And I will just note that the Prosecution does not accept or agree with the placement of the Convicts Battalion, but I'm not sure we'll come back to that or not. But overall this shows the structure from the supreme commander, and I take it that's Mr. Boban; correct? Mr. Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's Mr. Mate Boban, this box which reads "Supreme Commander." And at that moment, he was alone there, without anybody around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And beneath him we have the "Defence Department," and that was headed by Mr. Stojic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojic was there until the 15th of November, 1993, I believe, from the 3rd of July, 1992, if I'm not mistaken. If I am, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that's right. And the Main Staff, of course, through 1992 and at least up until about November of 1993, the head of the Main Staff or the command -- the number-one commander, so to speak, was either you or Mr. Praljak; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can be more accurate. That would be better. On the 24th of July, 1993, I handed over my duty to General Praljak. And on the 9th of November, 1993, he handed it over to General Roso. That was his last day on duty. He left on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we can agree and confirm that the special units, at least, or special units called the Bruno Busic, the Vitezovi, and the Ludvig Pavlovic, were linked to and, some would say, the assets of the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are units subordinate to the staff, that's what they were called, in the Yugoslav People's Army. So they were at the disposal of the Main Staff, rather than the operative zone, until they are attached to the operative zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you now to look and the courtroom to look in Sanction at an excerpt of your Blaskic testimony on this matter. And the Chamber's seen this before, but I must say I did find it to be a rather good and concise outline of these matters that you presented. I just want to go through it with you briefly. We've already talked about your measures to accede to and speed up the establishment of brigades of the Croatian Defence Council, and then it goes on to say: "Furthermore, there was a reorganisation of the military territorial division or, rather, the creation of operative zones. "Therefore, I now wish to present to you a diagram of the structure of the HVO in the period from 1992 until the end of 1993," which has been marked in this case as the document we just looked at, 11123: "The Decree on Armed Forces stipulated that the commander-in-chief was at the head of the army. "His administrative office comprised the Defence Department, and within the Defence Department, as an operative department, was the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council. "So I shall repeat this. The supreme commander was at the head of the army. The administrative section was called the Defence Department." Now, let's pause there. Everything -- you agree with and stand by your Blaskic testimony as to all those matters?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't put it like that. I didn't say that the commander-in-chief was in the Defence Department. The Main Staff was in the Defence Department, but the supreme commander was outside, and that's how it is represented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff is an integral part of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Well, it may have been translation, sir, because what's on the page, I'll be corrected, I'm sure, if I'm wrong, is a verbatim taken -- lifted directly out of the transcript of your testimony, so with apologies to interpretation, it may have been misheard: "The supreme commander was at the head of the army, the administrative section was called the Defence Department. "Within the Defence Department, there was a Main Staff as the operative part." You agree with all that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "The Main Staff had direct communications with the commands of the operative zones. There was the operative zone with its seat in Mostar, the operative zone with its seat in Tomislavgrad, the operative zone with its seat in Vitez, and the operative zone with its seat in Orasje: "A certain number of brigades, battalions, and other units were directly linked to each operative zone." And we're not going to go through those now: "As for the Main Staff, the first professional units of the Croatian Defence Council were directly linked to them, that is to say, the Bruno Busic Regiment, the Vitezovi, the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion." And you stand by all that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and that's why I drew the schematic the way I drew it. But if you want me to add, the Operative Zone of Orasje, on the 15th of October, 1992, was integrated into the command structure of the Main Staff. Until that time, it was separate and part of the Bosnian Posavina community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And before we leave this particular aspect, and if we had -- we don't need to look back at it, necessarily. But when you had the "Supreme Commander" box that we had up before, that was Mr. Boban from at least the time that you arrived in April of 1992, and continued to be the case until at least the end of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be more correct to say February 1994. I believe that he was replaced by Mr. Zubak then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. And I did say "at least until the end of 1993," just to try to avoid getting into a debate with you, but you're absolutely right. February 1994, and I believe he was actually replaced by a presidential council, of which Mr. Zubak was the head; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could look -- pause briefly on Exhibit P11124, the next exhibit after the one we were just looking at a moment ago, P11124. In your Blaskic testimony, you likewise presented a chart of the organisation of the Defence Department, headed by Mr. Stojic. Do you see that? Do you see that, sir, and do you still stand by that as an accurate portrayal of the structure?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not an accurate portrayal of the structure. It wasn't my intention here to present the structure of the Department of Defence. I only wanted to show how an administration was organised; namely, the Military Police Administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you don't disagree, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because there are elements missing here, such as assistants, et cetera. Some administrations were added that are of no special significance, but the Military Police Administration has been highlighted. But this isn't the original structure of the Department of Defence, nor was it my intention to present it here, because lots of things are missing; assistants, deputy, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you off for now. Sorry, you know our time is precious. This is the chart that you presented under oath, titled "Chart of the HVO Structure, 1992-1993." And I understand, sir, almost any chart could show more detail. But as far as this chart goes, you previously confirmed it under oath as accurate, and you would agree with that today, wouldn't you? Excuse me. I don't think we need any answers from the Defence. Mr. Stojic just said, no, out loud in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was waiting, but this isn't the way it was. You know yourself -- we've been here for four years on trial. You know that there wasn't such a structure. Thank you very much. I apologise for butting in like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer. As far as I remember, I didn't say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, General Petkovic. The Trial Chamber is asking the other accused not to interfere in the cross-examination. Mr. Scott is putting a question to the general, and it is for the general to answer. Now, if this does have a side-effect, that is another matter. General Petkovic, the document Mr. Scott is showing you is seemingly a document which you presented when you testified under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that the figure 9 is mentioned here. This means that you must have prepared several documents. I always look at the documents in your language to see whether they've been translated properly into English. In your language, I discover that as far as what you said regarding the military police, where it says "HVO" and the operative zones in the document, in your language you have put a dotted line between the operative zone and the battalions of the military police. In the English version, this is not a dotted line. This is a hyphen. Why was there a dotted line in the text in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is how I wanted to show the provisions of the Decree on the Structure of the Military Police, as adopted in December 1992, which means that the 2nd Battalion was carrying out its duties in Tomislavgrad OZ, the 3rd Battalion in OZ Mostar, the 4th Battalion in the territory of OZ Vitez, and the last one wasn't a battalion at the time, only a company, and it was active in OZ Orasje. That's the meaning of these dotted lines. This is in accordance with the document adopted on the 26th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having clarified this. Let me finish. I listened carefully to the question put by the Prosecutor concerning the documents, and the Prosecutor re-read to you what you had stated during your former testimony. I must say that this made me reflect on this. You said that the supreme commander, Mr. Boban -- everybody understood that. But then you added that the administrative section was called "Defence Department." I understand what this is. But then you added, and Mr. Scott read this out slowly, what you stated, you said that within this there was the Main Staff regarding operational issues. And I don't understand this, because you are saying that the Defence Department is administrative, but inside it there is an operational component of the Main Staff which is part of the Defence Department. I must say that I don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, if you read the Decree on the Armed Forces of the HZ-HB, you will read that the Department of Defence carries out staff duties for the president or the Presidency or, to simplify, for the commander-in-chief. And then there's another item for the carrying out of staff duties. In the framework of the Defence Department, the Main Staff is established or shall be established. It is logical that the Main Staff inside the Defence Department proclaims itself -- and it doesn't need to proclaim itself because it is a staff body, an operative body, and will carry out such activities upon the request of the commander-in-chief. And that's what the Decree on the Armed Forces says. And in the first part, it is also graphically represented like that. You may be confused by the fact that I didn't place the Main Staff inside the same box as the Defence Department, and instead draw a line between them showing a link. The Main Staff is a staff body and an operational body doing such work for the commander-in-chief. We can return to that and check, and you will see that it is an accurate depiction of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: In the Croatian Army and in the JNA, was it -- was there the same structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the Croatian Army, there was a main staff organised in the same way. It was an operative body of the supreme commander. In the JNA, there was the so-called -- there was the so-called Main Staff of the JNA. It was also a staff body of the Supreme Command. The JNA had a supreme command at the time, so there was some of them who formed part of that Supreme Command, and this General Staff -- Main Staff was the operative body to produce at the lowest level. So you can understand this, it was like a staff within an operative zone or staff within a brigade. It was involved in operative duties on behalf of the supreme commander in the HVO and in the Republic of Croatia. And Serbia or Yugoslavia had this so-called Supreme Command, and this staff performed duties -- worked for the needs of this Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of completeness, was it the same structure in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the ABiH, yes, there was this General Staff or, rather, they called it the Staff of the Supreme Command. We called it the Main Staff, and the Serbs called it the General Staff. The JNA used this term that was, for example, the nature of the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. General Halilovic was the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, I was the Chief of Staff of the HVO Main Staff, and I don't know who occupied that position in Serbia at the time; Perisic, for example, if he was the Chief of the General Staff, or perhaps it was someone else. All these bodies were staff bodies. They were involved in work that was carried out on behalf of the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think there might have been -- either Mr. Petkovic may have misspoke, or there may have been a mistranslation, but I don't believe Mr. Halilovic was ever the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. Or maybe I misheard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir? In any event, that's what I heard at one point. You were talking about --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Halilovic was the Chief of the Main Staff -- of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Perhaps there was some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to turn to Exhibit P04527, P04527.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it at the beginning of my binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not going in numerical order, sir, and I'm not sure I can tell you exactly. Probably more in the second half. 4527.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand. Sir, my question here is not so much about the content of the document, other than the list of names that we see here. For the record, this is a communication or order from a commander in the military police, dated the 26th of August, 1993. And if you look at the nine names -- let me first ask -- let me first pause at Mr. Stanko Matic. Can you just remind us of the position held by Mr. Matic as of the 26th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanko Matic was General Zarko Tole's deputy, the deputy of the commander [as interpreted] of the Main Staff. You knew that at the Main Staff we had a commander. That was the structure at the time. So he was the deputy, General Tole's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really have to correct the transcript. Line 16, it says "Commander of the Main Staff," whereas the general, in fact, said "the Chief of the Main Staff." So Stanko Bozic [as interpreted] was Zarko Tole's deputy or, rather, he was the deputy of the Chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stanko Matic, not Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, putting aside the military police --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The translation in line 22 is wrong again. I said Stanko Matic was the deputy of the Chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Putting aside, sir, the military police, would you agree with me this list of nine persons gives us a -- essentially a list of the very top of the HVO military and defence structure, as of August 1993, either in the Defence Department, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Bozic, Mr. Lucic, or in the operations of the Main Staff, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Petkovic, et cetera? This gives us really the main players, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the main players in the Defence Department or in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions in this relation -- excuse me, in relation to this structure and what we've been talking about so far. From the documents that I've seen, sir, the HVO command and reporting structure essentially involved a daily report up the chain. And by "up the chain," I mean if you want to say starting at the lower levels, and I won't go too low, but for present purposes, you had a daily report from the company commander to the brigade commander, from the brigade commander to the operative zone commander, from the operative zone commander to the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a principle that one had to abide by, but there were cases in which this principle wasn't respected. But that was the principle that was in force in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it was required, wasn't it, that the commander at each level would have to sign off on this report or approve the report, the content of the report, or, of course, if the commander, himself, was not available, then someone who was authorised to act on his behalf, a deputy or some such person, a person in authority would have to sign off that the content was, so far as they knew, at least, true and accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it depended on the nature of the report. If it was treated as a regular operative report, then it would be drafted by an operations officer who was on duty at the time. Sometimes he would put his name at the bottom of the document, because it was really the operations officer, and sometimes the commander's name would be put down, and it would be sent in that form. So operative officers would sign reports when they were on duty, and they would forward them up the chain of command from brigades to the operative zone and then up towards the Main Staff. The commander of an operative zone would, on occasion, sign the document if he was present there, if his name was placed on the document. But usually those in the operative service on duty had to draft these reports, and they had the right to forward such reports, only the reports they received from others. They didn't have the right to assess certain situations or draw conclusions. They would draft the final reports and then forward them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If Mr. Siljeg represented the situation this way, that he, as the operative zone commander, if he was present at the time, it would be he that would sign off on the reports before they went out, or if he was not there, then his deputy would do that for him, that would be the general practice, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it was an operative report, then Mr. Siljeg's name could be there, without him having signed the document, and it would then be sent. The operative officer would sign operative reports. At the end of his shift, he would draft an operative report. He would then inform Siljeg of the report, or, rather, any other commander present. Siljeg might sign it, but not necessarily. It could have been signed on his behalf, and then it could have been forwarded in that form. So it wasn't necessary for each such report to be signed by the commander of the operative zone. The operative officer communicates with the operative officer in the Main Staff, and they send these reports to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And you and Mr. Praljak, at the time that you were either number one or number two, so to speak, you were generally available to your commanders, weren't you? They could reach you if they wanted to, normally, by telephone, by radio, by some means; you were generally available to your commanders, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each and every commander who felt the need to come and discuss certain matters would have to be received. If a commander said --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I'm going to have to begin -- you know our time is precious, and I'm trying to be patient and I haven't been cutting you off, but I'm going to have to begin doing that more, I'm afraid. I'm sorry if that's discourteous. But not just to come to you, sir, but you were available to -- by communication. For example, Mr. -- if Mr. Siljeg represented that he was, for the most part -- and of course there were exceptions, but for the most part he was able to pick up the telephone at any time and reach you by phone, you would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would phone me. He had a phone. His duty was to phone whenever he felt that he had to have contact with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, but the answer to my question is, Yes, one word, Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But you're talking about him coming by using the phone. That's not how it's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, there could be any number of means. I started my question to you, and I'm not going to spend time arguing with you about his, but I first simply asked you: You were available to your commanders by various means of communication, whether it was telephone, radio, face to face, you were generally available to your commanders. I believe you said, Yes. I further put to you that, in addition, generally speaking, one could pick up the phone and reach you, and your answer just now was, Yes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the course -- we've heard in the course of your testimony, and in the testimony of others, for that matter, that you obviously weren't sitting at your desk at the HVO headquarters all the time. We know you were in Geneva, you were in Zagreb, you were in Split, you were in Grude, you were in Vitez, you were in Kiseljak. When either you or Mr. Praljak would not be physically present at HVO headquarters, how would people trying to reach you or needing to be in communication with you, how would they reach you or communicate with you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was possible to find out through the Main Staff where we were at the time. And if there was a phone number, they could find out where we were, and they would then phone the number. If I was in Sarajevo, I couldn't be reached. If I was in Geneva, I couldn't be reached. But if I was in Citluk, then he'd have a look in the telephone directory and phone the number in Citluk and ask the commander if the general was there, Can I speak to him, he would say, and that's how he could establish contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I dare to say you could be reached in Geneva and other places. I mean, people could find you if they wanted to. Mr. Petkovic is attending meetings in Geneva this week. He can be reached through the Croatian Ministry of Defence, he can be reached at Hotel so-and-so. Surely people could reach you. You're an important man. People needed to be able to reach you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one phoned me throughout that period of time, no one was provided with the number. When necessary, I would go to the Croatian Embassy and establish contact. On the 21st of January, for example, with the HVO --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On the 24th of January. Interpreter's correction, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies for cutting across.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's just talk about some of the locations you did go within Bosnia and Herzegovina. You spent -- you made a number of visits, from the documentation, to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. You went to Vitez and met with Mr. Blaskic on occasion. How many times can you tell us that you were in Vitez in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six or seven times. I might be able to remember the dates when I was there. There were conversations, discussions, with Halilovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Six or seven times. And can I ask you, approximately how many times in 1993 were you in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a number. I went to Kiseljak quite frequently because of the duties I had with regard to UNPROFOR or, rather, the international community, and also to get out the wounded, because we had a base where we had received the wounded, and this base was located in Kiseljak, and that's where we evacuated them from in Central Bosnia. But I really couldn't provide you with a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A dozen times, 15 times, 20 times?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty times for sure, perhaps even twenty-five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you were in Vitez or in Kiseljak, how would the people at your headquarters operations in Herzegovina, how would they communicate with you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a telephone line between the Kiseljak Main Staff and the Vitez Main Staff. It has been shown here in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, not just between the Kiseljak Main Staff and Vitez, but there were phone communications between headquarters in Herzegovina and Vitez, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone headquarters, and communications directly from Herzegovina headquarters to Kiseljak HVO, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two lines with Central Bosnia. One was with Vitez, and the other was with Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And apart from -- or in addition to telephone communications, sir, between the Herzegovina headquarters and both the Vitez and Kiseljak, there was Paket communication, wasn't there? And we've seen many of those in the course of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, when you travelled on your official duties through Bosnia-Herzegovina, you would keep your headquarters operations informed as to your whereabouts and where you could be reached. It would be irresponsible to do otherwise, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So if you were travelling, for example, in one of your 20 or so trips to Kiseljak, you would have said to your duty officer or your aide, whoever, or more than one, probably, you would say, I'm going to Kiseljak, I'm going to be there for the next three days, I can be reached through the Kiseljak HVO or through the operations there, something like that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would have been sufficient to say, I'm going to Kiseljak. Everyone has the telephone directory for Kiseljak and knows the number in Kiseljak, and that is the number that would be used. It is not necessary to mention anyone. It would be sufficient to say, I'm going to Kiseljak -- or, rather, it was my duty to tell my commander, I'm going to Kiseljak, or I'm going to Sarajevo, I'm going here or there, and then they could know how I could be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to touch, sir, moving forward, to subordination. And there's been quite a bit of testimony on that, and it may be -- it may be that it seems relatively clear, at least from your perspective, so I'm not going to spend a lot of time on it. But subordination involved one -- putting one unit that was not normally under someone's command in the day-to-day course of events, but putting that unit subject to the command and control of somebody else; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. A unit that wasn't a part of a given structure, but was sent to the structure, would then be subordinated. It was a unit that was part of Establishment A, and it was then sent to Establishment B, and it would be subordinated to Establishment B. So it wasn't part of that structure, but it had to temporarily, at least, become part of that structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, wouldn't you, sir, that, in fact, in the HVO every unit had to be under somebody's control; it could not exist on its own and act on its own?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have an HVO organisational unit, it has its own commander, it has its command structure, and if that is the case, then naturally it's under the control of the person who is at the head of that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could look, just to clarify or confirm that point, at -- in Sanction, it's number 4, for my case manager. This is what you said in Kordic, sir: "Every unit had to be under somebody's control; it could not exist on its own and act on its own." And you stand by that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only organisational units that listed as HVO units. If there were any other units of any other kind, well, then they weren't part of our structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of professional and special units, I believe, again, we can touch -- pass through that quite quickly. But, again, the principle was essentially the same. As we spoke, excuse me, a few moments ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I have a major follow-up question. General Petkovic, the Prosecutor's question was an important one, and you answered it. Well, to make it clearer, listen carefully. In the geographical zone of a brigade, if there is a Unit A, a Unit B, a Unit C, or possibly a unit that would be a D unit, in your view, is it so that the brigade commander in this zone has authority over A, B, C, and D units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it would be necessary to discuss the location in question. If it's a separate municipality and there's a brigade commander and another HVO unit that isn't his unit, well, then he would be in command of that unit. Naturally, it would be necessary to draft the relevant orders stating that they were being subordinated to him. However, if we take the Vitez area, it's a specific area. There's a brigade there, the military police headquarter is there, there's a special purposes unit there. In such a case, the brigade commander wouldn't have authority over those units in Vitez, and police would be the higher command or the commander of the operative zone who would have such authority. So it depended on the situation. It was different, depending on the location. As a rule, all the units in a given area should be placed under the command, at least temporarily while they are there, of one commander. No one should act independently and as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we have a few minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to touch briefly, then, because I don't want to spend too much time on it, but on the professional units, if we could go to -- in Sanction, to slide 5. I think this sums it up. Again, sir, from your testimony in the Blaskic case: "Professional units were linked to the Main Staff, and they could have carried out assignments issued by the Main Staff, but they could also have been subordinated to a certain commander to carry out assignments on his orders in a certain zone ... "So I'm claiming and stating that they were linked to the Main Staff and the Main Staff had either the right to use them on their own or to subordinate them to another commander, a commander of an operative zone who could use them on the basis of his own needs and tasks, and we know what the subordination of a unit means. This subordination involves the responsibility of the commander and the responsibility of those who are being subordinated to him." And you would stand by that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as an example, just to take one example, and I think it came up, perhaps yesterday, or some day in the last day or two -- it wasn't yesterday, but it came up. The Vitezovi unit, which was one of these professional units that was in Central Bosnia, and I believe you testified in both Blaskic and Kordic that the Vitezovi, for example, during most of 1993, was subordinated to Mr. Blaskic, but, in any event, that there was no one who could have controlled the Vitezovi during that period except you and Mr. Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 15th of January, Colonel Blaskic had exclusive control over Vitezovi. I couldn't have control over them, because from April, I couldn't gain access to that territory to gain an idea of what was happening. That's why it was subordinated. If you haven't got an overview of it, then it has to be subordinated to someone who can have an idea of the situation, and this was the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. It's the order of the 15th of January, which you have, which refers to all elements of combat organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, sir. But it's also your testimony, and you made it very clear in Blaskic, that throughout that time-period, as the commander of the Main Staff, as the Chief of the Main Staff, you also retained, throughout that time-period, responsibility. It was subordinated to Blaskic, but you also maintained responsibility and authority over that unit, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified that I did not separate it from the Main Staff, because if I had done that, it would have become part of the structure of OZ Central Bosnia and I would have lost it in the structure of the Main Staff, as shown earlier. So I maintain that it still was a unit of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can finish this topic, Mr. President, before the break. I just have one or two more questions, and then I'll be changing topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just finishing on this concept, then, of control, as much as we've been able to cover it so far this morning, we sometimes hear of units being out of control. But in reality, sir, units were under always -- virtually always under somebody's control. They couldn't, in fact, act on their own; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier, and I'm still saying, and you can find that in my documents, all organised units. And when I say "organised," I mean those that were established in the HVO in its official documents, they were under control. All units or groups of persons that were not established that way were not under the control of any commander of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look, please, on Sanction -- in Sanction at slide number 6, your testimony in the Kordic case under oath, page 26746: "Q. So there can be no question, can there, of units operating in Vitez terrorising the local inhabitants and being out of control because they were either under your control or they had been specifically subordinated to Blaskic, you would say? "A. Your Honours, yes. Every unit had to be under somebody's control; it could not exist on its own and act on its own." And you stand by that now, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are HVO units that must be under control. Outside the HVO, we have no control over units. So this referred to HVO units, irrespective of their size or name, but they were HVO units that must be under control. Other units that we did not establish or didn't provide rules for them in our documents could -- could act otherwise. We could have -- there could have been incidents with them, et cetera. So I was referring to HVO units, our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand. Your Honour, that would be a time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the Stojic Defence has something to say about a technical question relating to a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Thank you. I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Scott. I would just like to point it out to the Trial Chamber and have it recorded in the transcript that the document that he showed, and that is document 11123, which is a schematic of the structure of the HVO for the period from 1992 to 1993, is mistranslated into English, and that document is an exhibit as 4D618. And the correct translation has an IC number, 1169. Thank you, Your Honours. That's what I had to say, for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And there is no dispute about that. It's been -- counsel have discussed it before. The Prosecution has taken the position that since it was -- if it's an admitted exhibit in another case, that we couldn't unilaterally change it because it's a matter of Tribunal record. But we agree that's what it would properly show.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn to something that you touched on your very first day, and that is you agreed that -- in fact, Ms. Alaburic put the question to you this way: "In a well-organised society, do civilian authorities exert control over the military?" And your answer was: "The civilian authorities do excerpt control the military." And that was the case in the HVO, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was set up that way to provide for the possibility of controlling the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we just pause briefly a little bit further, a lengthier part of your testimony on slide number 7 in Sanction: "Q. Still, if we are trying to defined the position that applies to other social communities, irrespective of the concrete situation in Croatia, would you say that it is normal and that the civilian authorities should, indeed, control the military? "A. Absolutely. It would be bad if it was the other way around or if the army controlled itself. That army would be good for nothing, or far be it for anybody from the military to control the civilian authorities. That would be bad." Staying on that topic, sir, would it be fair to say, and I'm going to put it to you, that in connection with the civilian control of the HVO military, that the three principal civilians having such power or control were Mr. Boban, as the president of Herceg-Bosna, as commander-in-chief, Mr. Stojic, as head of the Defence Department, and Mr. Prlic, as head of the government? That would be the case, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban had the right to directly control. Mr. Stojic was in the system of the military, and Mr. Stojic could exert indirect control through the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Prlic, as head of the government, exercised substantial authority or influence over defence and military matters, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic was -- headed the provisional authority of the HVO, and his influence was limited by the Decree on the Armed Forces and by the organisational structure of his administrative bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm not talking now about, necessarily, issuing directly military orders, but you'd have to agree with me, wouldn't you, that in the HVO authorities, as relates to military and defence matters, there couldn't be three more powerful people than Mr. Boban, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Prlic, could there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it is set out in the -- laid out in the Decree on the Armed Forces. It defines the powers of the head of the Department of Defence and other government officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I'm sorry, my learned friend Mr. Scott. Your Honour, can I just say for the record that slide number 7 refers to transcript page 49297-98 [Realtime transcript read in error "4929798"] it would be useful, perhaps, and a matter for my learned friend, either to have all the extracts that are in Sanction with the slide number labelled, then would obviate the need to refer every time to the transcript number. Or, alternatively, always when my learned friend refers to the Sanction slide number, also to give the transcript page number. Sometimes today it's been given, sometimes we haven't got the record. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, well, it might be useful if when you give the number of the slide and you give us the transcript page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: On the transcript, we have many, many pages, but we don't have 4 million, as indicated here, almost 5 million. Perhaps it would be good to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's true. In terms of the current slide, which I believe is slide number 7, it should be transcript 49297, continuing to 98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what I was about to put to you was: In fact, Mr. Stojic, in a sense, had -- in terms of the structures that you've told us about and what we otherwise know, Mr. Stojic had a relationship to Mr. Boban, as commander-in-chief, but at the same time Mr. Stojic was the head of an executive department that was part of Mr. Prlic's government, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when Mr. Stojic want to do have funding, and logistical support, and guns and food and medical supplies, it was through the government -- he had to go through the HVO government, the HVO HZ-HB, to seek those resources, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The funds for procuring everything were provided at the level of the HVO authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, returning -- or staying on Mr. Stojic for a moment, Mr. Stojic -- you considered Mr. Stojic, in fact, to be your superior and a person in the structure of things who had more power than you did; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my superior. That is normal, because I was in the structure of the Department of Defence. I was responsible to him for my duties. And by virtue of his being a member of the Cabinet, and I'm not sure which positions you mean, but clearly due to that he could -- he had wider scope of powers and was able to carry out more activities than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify for a moment, to avoid possible objection, we do know, and I think we can agree, that the proper terminology until, perhaps, late 1993 was he was the head of the Defence Department. And it wasn't until some later reorganisation that these were renamed ministries or the "Ministry of Defence." But you frequently refer to Mr. Stojic as "minister," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct to call him "head" for the time-period until the ministry was established. From that point on, he was minister. I'll try to call him "head" in one period and "minister" in the period when ministries were established, when -- that is, at the time of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we can go to slide number 8, which is your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, excuse me. Mr. Petkovic, you have said that Mr. Stojic had authority over the military indirectly. Could you specify what you mean by "indirectly"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Stojic was no commander, so he didn't have direct authority, but he was at the head of the Defence Department. So in line with his position, his responsibilities and duties, he had links with the military and duties with respect to the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On that point, sir, if we could then look briefly at slide number 8, which is some of your testimony from the Kordic case; transcript page 26749. You testified under oath in that case, sir, and you said: "... Bruno Stojic, who was above me, because he was my minister, and his powers were much larger than mine." And that remains your position and your assessment; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite logical that a person in that position has greater powers than me. I had powers within the chain of command, and he had powers with regard to the Department of Defence, which later became the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it from everything you've said so far, sir, that you accepted -- in fact, on a regular daily basis, if you will, as your regular practice, you accepted Mr. Stojic as your superior?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of his position and my position in the Department of Defence, it is clear that he was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would it also be fair to say, sir, that you had a good relationship with Mr. Stojic, or the two of you together, both professionally and personally?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that this originates from the position? Well, people are not necessarily in good relations because they are in certain positions, but, yes, we did have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention with regard to the transcript. Page 46, line 3, in Mr. Petkovic's answer, the end is missing. He said "he was my superior with regard to certain matters." This "certain matters" part is missing in the transcript. Mr. Petkovic can confirm whether I'm right or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "superior," the minister of defence is the superior of the chief of Main Staff, because the Main Staff is an integral part of the Ministry of Defence, and that is why the Department of Defence is headed by one person, which makes that person the superior of everybody else in that department.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I wish to support Ms. Nozica. This was an incomplete interpretation of General Petkovic's sentence, and I can confirm that Ms. Nozica is right. The last part of this sentence is missing "in certain matters," and the general was only asked to corroborate whether or not he said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said there were some matters in which I was directly responsible to the head of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
