utterances.text: And I suppose, sir -- based on these interventions, can you tell us those matters in which you were directly responsible to, if you will -- the word you just now said, you said, I was directly responsible to the head of the Department of Defence in some matters. Which matters were those?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a simple answer. Everything but operative matters; that is, the entire activity of the Department of Defence, except for operative matters, where a person in my position was linked to the supreme commander within that line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And staying on this leadership -- civilian leadership group, Mr. Praljak testified in the Tuta Stela case under oath, and we've seen it before in this courtroom, that it was, indeed, Mr. Boban, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Prlic who were the prime players in that respect. Would you agree with Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were the highest-ranking persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm just trying to cut through a few things, sir. Sorry for the delay. Just following on this topic, then, you also testified on your first day that the objectives -- the overall strategy of Herceg-Bosna, the overall objectives were set by the civilian authorities and communicated to the military; correct? And we can look at -- we can look at slide 9. That comes from your testimony in this case, 49292-93. You agree with that and stand by it? It's your testimony in this very case, so I assume, sir, you stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain to the Judges, sir, how were these objectives, then, set by the civilian authorities, how would they be communicated to you in the Main Staff? In other words, how did you get your marching orders?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic objective at the political level was the defence of the Croatian people in the area where Croats live in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the basic objective, and that is why, in Bosnia-Herzegovina and later on in the part called Herceg-Bosna, the defence of the Croatian people against the Serbian aggression was organised then. That was the basic objective of the creation of Herceg-Bosna and of the establishment of its structures. It is normal that defence will be performed, for the most part, by the armed forces, and others will participate in line with their capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But beyond that, sir, there must have been times in 1992/1993, apart from, Go forth and defend Herceg-Bosna, that certain policy decisions were made, certain strategic decisions were made, Let's go in this direction, Let's go in that direction, Let's launch a major offensive, Let's put most of our eggs in this basket over here, or, Let's go in the other direction over here. When those decisions were made by the civilian authorities, how would they be communicated to you? How did you -- did you get a telephone call from someone, did you receive a memo, did you go to meetings of the government where these decisions were announced to you? How did you get your marching orders?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which offensive you mean. I don't think we can make up offensives here. We should be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't want to lose time debating that with you at the moment. Operations. There was a military operation, and someone decides there has to be, at a broad strategic level, at least as far as I know -- my understanding of how most armies work during war -- World War II, do the Allies -- do they land at Normandy, or do they work their way up from Italy, or both? Those decisions were ultimately made politically. Roosevelt and Stalin and Churchill, they would decide and they would say, Here's the basic plan, this is what we're trying to accomplish. So who -- how were those decisions communicated to you by your civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just launch an objection at this point. That example, for instance, now, Mr. Scott is testifying, and there's a certain presumption. We actually don't know that, who was actually making the decisions at that level. So if this is just an illustration, I think Mr. Scott would need to demonstrate that he has actual personal knowledge and from where he's getting this information. I don't think this is so notorious of a fact that we all can just assume it and that the Trial Chamber can accept it as an adjudicated fact, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, Mr. Karnavas is questioning the fact that during World War II, the Normandy landing was not decided by Churchill, Stalin and Roosevelt. Maybe he forgot about General de Gaulle, but maybe he was right to forget about him. Whatever the case may be, the question is a very interesting question. When a marching order is given under military authority which stems from the civilian authority, Mr. Scott is asking you how things work, and he illustrates this by providing a well-known example drawn from World War II. What do you have to say to this? It's your answer that is interesting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I believe a better example would be one from Herceg-Bosna or Bosnia-Herzegovina than an example from the Second World War. We had to defend the western part of Herceg-Bosna first, and Mr. Boban took the decision that this part must be defended. And so we started to set up defence lines around Livno and Tomislavgrad, et cetera. When we had to cross the Neretva and liberate some areas occupied by the Serbs, the decision was taken to launch such an operation, and then preparations began and the operation was launched. When events unfolded, when the HVO in certain areas was in a poor situation, then measures were sought to defend Croats in these areas. So there are specific activities in each area. And, of course, the authorities of Herceg-Bosna followed the events and took decisions to defend some areas and defend the interests or start negotiations with the other side to stop the conflicts between the ABiH and the HVO. This is what went on in Herceg-Bosna at the level of government, at the level of the military, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me be a bit more concrete, based on that. And if we have time, sir, we'll get to -- we'll have to get to some of these documents, but isn't it the fact that you attended a number of government meetings, and when I say "government" now, I'm talking about the body headed by Mr. Prlic, the HVO HZ-HB, and you would give a briefing on military matters and defence matters. And there were times then the government would come back to you and say, All right, thank you for this briefing. Here's what we want to do, and go forth and implement this decision. That's how it worked, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended three or four governmental sessions that I was invited to. I briefed them on the military situation in certain areas. At certain points of time, decisions were taken by the government according to which the HVO and other forces should take measures in order to protect the interests of the Croatian people in that area in order to mount a defence and to discuss matters with the other side, in order to find an overall solution to the problems we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we have time, sir, I'm going to suggest to you that it was more than three times. I think it was a significantly larger number than that. But if we have time, we'll come back to that. I want to then go back to --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there less than three times. Perhaps it wasn't five occasions. I accept that I was at every meeting that I attended. We can go into that in detail. I have the time to do so. We have the time to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Petkovic, there's no doubt that I wish we had a lot more time. I don't think there's no one in the courtroom that doubts that. I want to go back to the question of HVO command and control. And you basically agree, sir, that during at least 1993, because I don't want to debate the entire time-period with you, but certainly in 1993, there was a working system of command and control in the HVO, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system, as such, existed on paper. However, on numerous occasions, the system wasn't implemented in the way it was intended to be implemented. So there were quite a few problems when it came to implementing that system, to actually bring that system to life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, no one's suggesting that it was perfect, and I suspect that -- everyone always wants to talk in here about NATO armies, and I suspect even in NATO armies, so-called, they are not perfect systems. But it was the case, wasn't it, that a chain of command had been put in place, and it was in working order, and you've said so before, and that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A chain of command had been established. As to whether it was functional or not, well, that is debatable. It was functional to the extent that it was possible to make it functional at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at slide number 10, please, slide number 10, which comes from your testimony in the Kordic case, transcript page 26861: "Q. And that shows, General, if I may suggest to you, that the chain of command was well identified, that it did what it was supposed to do, and that it operated in the manner that you would expect a military chain of command to operate in April of 1993. Would you agree with that?" Milivoj Petkovic's answer under oath: "Your Honours, I have always claimed that the chain of command had been put in place and that it was in working order. I continue to affirm that." And you continue to affirm your testimony under oath in the Kordic case, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had in mind the level that I functioned at with my immediate subordinates, so the Central Bosnian Operative Zone was what I had in mind and the headquarters there. So it was in that sense that the chain of command had been established. I didn't discuss lower levels. I was describing Blaskic and the problems of command he had, and I emphasised all the problems from that level, and at lower levels too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, actually, that's not -- that wasn't your testimony in the Blaskic case, because you said in Blaskic -- you said in Blaskic that, in fact, Mr. Blaskic never complained to you about lack of command and control; that, again, as far as you knew and as far as Mr. Blaskic represented to you, there were no complaints. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That concerned the Blaskic-Kordic relationship, but you should read what I said about Mr. Blaskic. I said there were command problems that he had. He took certain measures, he couldn't go there, there were poor communications, so he took measures in order to have operation groups to make it easier to command. So quite a lot was said about the command problems that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, we don't have a slide of this, but this is what you said in Kordic at page 26883: "And it's also true, General, I believe, that Blaskic made no comment about any kind of lack of command or control over the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, its sub-units, or the Vitezovi?" Milivoj Petkovic's answer: "No, Your Honours, there was no comment to the effect that he did not have control over the Vitezovi or the 4th Military Police Battalion. I never received any report until then or after that that either the military police or the Vitezovi were uncontrollable." That's the testimony you gave, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I stand by that. But the system of command -- the chain of command doesn't involve only these two units; far more than that. But as far as these two units are concerned, I stand by what I testified about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Petkovic, not to get too bogged down in this, because we have many other things to talk about, but the reason those particular two units were so important was because those were two of the units that were accused of committing many of the crimes in Central Bosnia. It was the 4th Battalion Military Police, by your own assessment, that committed the crimes in Ahmici. It was the Vitezovi which committed many crimes against Muslims in Central Bosnia in 1993. And you came and told this Tribunal that you never received any complaints from Mr. Blaskic in 1993 that either of these units were out of control, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that they were under control, but I didn't say that the Vitezovi had committed numerous crimes. All I said is that the Vitezovi were not in Ahmici, that they provided security for the command building for Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Vitezovi may not have been in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, but Pasko Ljubicic and the military police certainly were, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. You misunderstood me. I wanted to say that the military police was there, but the Vitezovi were not. According to what I was aware of at the time, they weren't in Ahmici. That's what I said in the trial, and I stand by that. I said that at the time the Vitezovi were 200 or 300 metres in front of the hotel, and it was at that line that they were providing security for the command of Colonel Blaskic, because he was 300 or 400 metres away from the ABiH towards the old part of Vitez, and that is where that hotel is, in fact, located.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, sir, just to finish on this specific example, not only -- not only was there no complaint from Mr. Blaskic about control of the Vitezovi and the 4th Battalion Military Police, but according to your testimony in Kordic at page 26885, Mr. Blaskic, after the actions in mid-April 1993, commended the behaviour of both of those units, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's been some issues raised in this case about alleged local political interference with or control of the HVO military. But in fact, sir, as you've already testified today, and in your experience, that wasn't true, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to object to this question now, because if my memory doesn't fail me, this is not what the witness said. However, if I'm mistaken, could my colleague Mr. Scott give us the necessary reference in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for one thing, and I'll move on to his testimony in the other cases, but one of the things he said this morning, for example, was he had put an end to the municipal staffs and to municipal control of the militaries, and that was what the reorganisation of the HVO military and brigades was partly all about. And he said he had brought that to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, if we can go to slide number 10 -- let's look at the Kordic case, let's look at the Kordic case, slide number 11, and Blaskic. In the Blaskic case, slide 11, page 24025, Milivoj Petkovic, under oath: "I wish to state the following: Civilian officials did not have any powers whatsoever in terms of commanding the military police or any units of the Croatian Defence Council." Your testimony in the Kordic case, 26675: "In my command, I never received any objection from any of the commanders under me that they received some orders from outside, that is, outside the HVO military chain of command structure." You testified not on one occasion, but on two occasions, under oath, that there was no outside political interference, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I testified about two levels, a military level in the operations zone and another level which was the political level that had to do with Mr. Kordic, and I said, and I stand by what I said, that I never received information from Blaskic about that level. And you can't include Mr. Kordic in the municipal level. I never received information that that level had influence on Mr. Blaskic. But in the case of Blaskic, I said that in Vitez they didn't consider him the commander of Vitez. That means that the people from Vitez didn't accept him as such. So let's leave the levels that I have testified about; Blaskic, the operations zone; Kordic, politics, which is higher than the municipal level. And at that level, with regard to the command of the operative zone, Siljeg, Lasic, or Blaskic couldn't be influenced by politics. But there were local brigades and so on and so forth, and then the relationship between the political structures and the brigade remained very strong there. So I wanted to clarify this matter of level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to correct something. Line 4 on the current page, it says that the witness said "in Vitezovi," whereas the witness said "in Vitez," in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we all accept that -- we know the context of the Kordic and the Blaskic cases involved directly Central Bosnia, but I put it to you, sir, that your testimony was broader than that. It evolved into a broader discussion, and you weren't distinguishing that. And I put to you, and I'm not going to read them to you again, but everyone can see them on the screens, you said, generally, civilian officials did not have any powers: "I never received any objection from any of the commanders under me that they would receive orders from outside." And as you have just said, that included Siljeg, Lasic, Blaskic, all the operative zone commanders, and none of them ever complained to you that they were getting local political interference, did they? Sir, you just said so; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, and I mentioned the relevant levels. I know what I said in my reports. I never said that someone was exerting an influence on Siljeg or Blaskic and Lasic, but at the level of operative -- or, rather, at the level of brigades, in each and every report it said that there was interference in the influence of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's not really exactly true, is it, sir, because Mr. Filipovic testified in this case, and Mr. Filipovic testified both in the Prlic case and in the Kordic case that, again, at the brigade level, he never received any directions or interference from outside the HVO chain of command. In Kordic, he said that at page 17070, as to military matters, the organisation, especially conduct, were "always within the chain of command, they were not commanded by politicians." Now, that's at the brigade level, sir, by a witness you called in this case, Mr. Filipovic; correct? Also, sir, while you're considering that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I know that, Mr. Karnavas. I'm trying to save a little bit of time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While you're considering that, sir, Mr. Filipovic said also in Kordic, 17138, that he never took orders from, he was never subordinated to any political or municipal leader. And you agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I never said that the chief was in command. I said there was influence that was exerted in various kinds. The chief didn't command the brigades. I was in charge. But we have said that influence was exerted on the brigades in various ways, but no one drafted orders for the brigades. But I can stand by what Filipovic said. When we refer to orders, we know what is at stake. When we say exerting an influence in various other ways, well, this means something else. That is not an order, but it is a manner of influencing the brigades in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look, please, at slide number 12, your testimony in the Kordic case at page 26805-06. Answer to the question: "Your Honours, the orders followed the chain of command vertically from the supreme commander down to the Main Staff. I didn't receive any orders outside of that. "Q. Did you receive orders or directives from other politicians other than Mr. Boban at any time during your service as head of the armed forces of the HVO? "A. No, Your Honours. Nobody outside this vertical chain of command, Boban, Stojic, issued orders to me or the army." And that's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying no one issued orders to me outside that chain of command. But you should understand the following: It has to do with issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I'm going to have to, Mr. Petkovic, with apologies, begin to start cutting you off somewhat, because our time is just too limited. I wish I could allow you more time. But let me be clear here. When you're talking about the chain of command in this instance, you're talking about the chain of command Boban, Stojic, Main Staff, correct, as you say in your answer here at page 26805-06 of Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and lower down to the operation zone. I think I said that. I must have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, just to finish on this topic, let me put some other testimony from Mr. Filipovic to you, and I'll ask you if you agree. More generally than this, would you agree -- do you recall that, in fact, the HDZ political party, as of June 1992, in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not particularly active, and, in fact, as Mr. Filipovic said in Kordic at page 17038, the HDZ party at that point in time, for practical purposes "had ceased to exist." You agree with him, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ had frozen its activities. I don't think that it had dismantled itself, but it had frozen its activities. So the HDZ didn't gather any levels at the lower, mid levels, or higher levels. So in the course of the war, it quite simply ceased to operate. But I don't think that that is tantamount to dismantling the HDZ, because after the war it continued with its work, it froze its work, suspended its work. It did not gather, it did not work, it didn't assemble, and it didn't take any decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, to close on this topic, if we can go to slide number 13, your testimony in Kordic at page 26804-05, the question which might have been put even in this case: "Q. Some of the international observers have speculated that the HVO army affairs were subject to pervasive political control exerted by the HDZ BiH? Is that true, that there was such control exerted by that political party?" Milivoj Petkovic, under oath: "Your Honours, that is not true. It is another matter that our supreme commander, Mr. Boban, was both the supreme commander and the president of the Croat community, subsequently Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and that, in point of fact, he was the man number one of the HDZ. But I do not see that the HDZ ever ran the army or the HDZ, as such, as a party, imposed itself on the military. And as far as I know, I think that the work of the party was frozen for a while." Which is actually consistent with what you said just a moment ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The people who were making the decisions in 1993, sir, was the military leadership inside the HVO Main Staff, and the HVO government, led by Mr. Prlic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please read that out again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Certainly. The people who were making the decisions in 1993, sir, because we've been talking about the HDZ as a political party, the people making the decisions was the military leadership inside the Main Staff, that is, you, Mr. Praljak, other senior staff perhaps, and the HVO government, and I'm talking about the HVO HZ-HB, headed by Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everyone took the relevant decisions within his own sphere of competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Staying in the political arena a bit, sir, I'm a bit confused, in fact, and we've touched on the HDZ, whether you were a member of the HDZ or not. You seem to -- I don't remember if you specifically addressed the question in this case or not. But, sir, in the Kordic case you testified -- and if we can look at slide 16. In the Kordic case, you testified, at page 26804: "Your Honours --" under oath: "Your Honours, I was not a member of any party at the time, because the decree even specified that we were prohibited from joining parties or creating parties. The only party at that time was the HDZ, and I was not a member of the HDZ." But when we have your curriculum vitae from the Croatian government or Croatian Army, which is marked as P08731, you say: "Since 1992, I have been a member of the HDZ." So can you tell us which of those statements is true and which one is false?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are true. At the time that I gave my testimony in the year 2000, I was no longer a member of the HDZ. That's what that refers to. In the Croatian Army, the work of the HDZ had been prohibited. I'm not sure when I was struck from the list, whether it was in 1998 or 1999. All of us who had become members of the HDZ were no longer members in the Croatian Army. I don't know whether it was in 1998 or 1999 our membership was terminated. I know that this, however, continued in the year 2000, when everyone had to leave the political parties. At the time that I gave that testimony, I wasn't an HDZ member, but I did join the HDZ, and I was also taken off the list of HDZ members at a subsequent date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. General Petkovic, I'm listening to your answers whilst remembering the questions put by the Prosecutor on the military police and on Ahmici. In the Blaskic case, you testified - this is well known because all this is now in the public domain - and the Prosecutor cross-examining you was Mr. Kehoe, unless I'm mistaken, who's now one of the Defence counsel for General Gotovina. And he asked you, at page 22524 in the French version - I don't have the English version, unfortunately, with me - and he asked you what Mr. Blaskic told you over the telephone as to what had happened in Ahmici. And this is what you answered: "Well, he assumed that among the police officers, at least among those who were in Ahmici, there were some who had behaved uncontrollably," out of control. What did this mean, exactly, because the Prosecutor is now asking questions as to the chain of command, and Blaskic, the commander of the operations zone, says that there are policemen who behave out of control. What did you mean in saying so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I received this information when visiting Central Bosnia, information according to which there was a group that was out of control, they acted willfully, and they didn't carry out the tasks assigned to them by the commander who was in command of the operation in Ahmici. I had Mr. Ljubicic in mind. So there were groups that were out of control and failed to act in accordance with the tasks assigned to them. That is what one has in mind here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But back then, you were the Chief of the Main Staff. You were the superior of Mr. Blaskic, hierarchically speaking, so also superior to these policemen that had been assigned to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is an unjustified conclusion. The Main Staff didn't command that way, nor did it command the action in Ahmici. The chain of command went as far as the operative zone. The Main Staff got involved to stop the operation in Central Bosnia and then took steps, together with the other side, to go there personally and calm down the situation to bring it back to normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time in April 1993, did you know that within the HVO, in all of its components, the military police, the military component - I won't go into detail on that - but that there were uncontrollable elements, rogue elements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, you cannot know that some elements are out of control. If we were able to identify them, we would remove them from the HVO or take other adequate steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I understand it, when Mr. Blaskic told you that the policemen in Ahmici were out of control, that was something you just learned, that was first news for you. Was it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I received that information only upon my second visit to Bosnia on the 28th or 29th of April, 1993. My first visit, on the 20th and 21st, wasn't an occasion when anything was said about Ahmici or anybody's behaviour there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your CV you say, and it's P08731 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric, what do you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. We cannot really hear Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you have to turn off -- switch off your microphone, because when there are too many mikes on, it doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation] [Interpretation] I switched it on. Is it better now? We can hear now. General, do you know that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Now we can no longer hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I don't know whether Mr. Scott's going to object, but what is -- what is happening here? We don't understand that the procedure simply allows some cross-examination by interjection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Coric, I thought you wanted to take the floor to address a problem in the transcript, but you're not allowed, at this stage of the proceedings, to ask questions of the witness who's testifying; namely, General Petkovic. If you have a substantial problem, you can address that when you call your own witnesses or when you testify in person. So as to substance, the general answers questions, gives his point of view, and you may contradict him later; but not now, and now is the stage when we have the Prosecutor and General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I'm intervening --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can no longer hear Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation] [Interpretation] We'll try this one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot work this way. We're getting strong interference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it better now? Yes, it is better. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I reacting to the question you asked about Ahmici. You asked such questions, and comments were made that are contrary to the decisions of some Trial Chambers and the final decisions of the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal. I'll be specific. This is about the Bralo case, a man who was directly involved in the Ahmici operation, who was not a member of the military police. And together with all Croats, he was released from prison during the night preceding the Ahmici operation and was a commander at Ahmici with other military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not acceptable. It's the microphone that had the right idea by cutting off Mr. Coric before he started. It's absolutely impermissible, in our submission, and he is not allowed to argue, he is not allowed to throw in comments, he's not allowed to interject questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, according to our procedure, you are not entitled to interject. My question was a very simple one. During Mr. Kehoe's cross-examination relating to a meeting between General Petkovic and Colonel Blaskic, Colonel Blaskic mentioned this, and General Petkovic told him what Blaskic had said. Now that the Tribunal ruled otherwise, that is another question, and you can submit your arguments then, when the time comes. The only point of interest now is to know what Blaskic had told General Petkovic, and General Petkovic confirmed that that was, in effect, what Blaskic had told him. Perhaps Blaskic had made a mistake, perhaps that was wrong. That is a totally different issue. You can address that when the time comes. This is not the right moment. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ahmici isn't part of the indictment, and we shouldn't be discussing that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The microphone isn't functioning properly. We cannot hear Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mine is functioning, and I sustain my objection, Your Honour. We invite Your Honour to tell Mr. Coric specifically that he is to sit down and say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, you must sit down and not say any more about it. There is no justification for this right now. You may address this issue when the time comes. This is not the right moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Petkovic, we now have to go back some minutes to the topic we were talking about, and that was your membership in the HDZ party. I want to suggest to you, sir, with great respect, that when you testified in previous cases, no one was particularly interested at that time about whether you were a member of the party in 1988 or 1999, that the important time was the time of these events in 1992, 1993, perhaps 1994. And if we look at your CV, and it is P08731, unfortunately the CV itself doesn't bear a date, but I've been scanning through it, and about the last date that I can see, a little below halfway down the second page in English, is you make reference to -- and you'll remember this, you'll know. This is your biographic -- this is your bio. You know: "In November of 1996, I assumed the duties of the deputy head of Osijek Military District." So we know the CV must have been written at least sometime after November of 1996, but you say on the last page, on the last line of the entire CV: "Since 1992, I have been a member of the HDZ." Now, I read that to mean that this document was created sometime in or after 1996 -- November 1996, that at least as of since 1992 and continuing since then, you were a member of the HDZ. Weren't you? Or as I said before, which of these statements is true and which one is false?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written in December 1996, I believe, this CV of mine, because I was required to submit it to the Personnel Administration. And I was a member of the HDZ starting from 1992, but I believe in 1998 or 1999, it was at the time when I was already in Dubrovnik, serving in Dubrovnik, I had been deleted from the list of members of the HDZ, because as the general --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, but time is precious, and I don't really care, for these purposes, what you did in 1998 or 1999. You were a member of the HDZ, you tell us now, even though you told the Court in Kordic -- and clearly you were talking about the importance -- once again, we have the whole transcript here and we can read out pages of context, if need be. We have the whole transcript right here. What you were talking about at the time was 1993: "I was not a member of any party at the time." Now, sir, you either lied to the Kordic Chamber or you lied on your curriculum vitae. Now, which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 or 1999, I ceased to be a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I don't care about 1998 or 1999. In 1993, you say -- in a document you say you created in -- excuse me, you say you created it in December 1996, and in that document you say: "Since 1992, I have been a member of the HDZ." And when you testified in this case -- in the Kordic case, and they were asking you about your membership at the time in question, you said that you were not. You gave false testimony to this Tribunal, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. The question in the Kordic case was not specific with regard to the time at which the general was or wasn't in the HDZ. I ask my learned friend not to misrepresent General Petkovic's statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated then that I was no longer an HDZ member, because in 1998 or 1999 I was -- I ceased to be a member of that party because, as a high-ranking officer of the Croatian Army, I couldn't be a member of a political party, and my status until then was frozen. We all were deleted from the list of members. When I gave evidence in the year 2000 - I don't remember which month it was - I really wasn't a member of any political party. But since 1992 or1991, whenever the war started, the army didn't accept for its officers to have positions in a political party. I'm not saying that I wasn't an HDZ member ever, because I was for 5 or 6 years, but I was deleted as I was told that I couldn't and all my documents stayed behind in Slavonia. I never got them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were since 1992, sir, by your own CV: "I have been a member since 1992." And, again, I have the transcript, and I beg to differ with my good friend Ms. Alaburic. I'm looking at page 26803. Questions are being asked about June 1992. Later on, Blaskic takes a different position in May 1994, whether there were some political officers in the army. And they're not talking about 1998 and 1999, sir. They're talking about the events in question. And you told -- you told Judge May and Judge Bennouna and Judge Robinson under oath in the Kordic case that you were not a member of the HDZ, when in your curriculum vitae you said you were. That's just the simple truth of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question has been answered, and, therefore, I object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During -- or at the time that I gave evidence, I had already been deleted from the listed members of HDZ. I joined that party in 1992, and I'm not denying that. That's why in 1996 -- or, that is, 1998, I wrote that I was deleted from the list of members, because, as a general, I couldn't have a status in a party. And we all got a document that we had been deleted. In 2002, at the very latest, everybody had to leave the party. So I was a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, we're not going to go on on this topic. We're going to end this topic except for this, my last question to you on this topic, unless the Judges want to pursue it further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me what the exact page number in the Kordic case is where he stated that he was not a member of the HDZ, because I have transcript page number 26803. Could you give me the exact page number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can assist. It's page, actually, 26804, lines 17 following: "Your Honours, I was not a member of any party at the time, because the decree even specified that we were prohibited from joining parties or creating parties. The only party at that time was the HDZ, and I was not a member of the HDZ." I must say, Ms. Alaburic, your objection is wholly unfounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I merely want to say that the time reference was not precise, because if the witness, in 2001, speaks about something that happened in 1998, that was also an event in the past.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I understood the Trial Chamber, when I gave evidence in the Kordic case, I was not a member of the HDZ. For two or three years, I had already been deleted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are trying our patience, because you are always repeating that, and you have been told many things that -- many times now that this is not the issue. And if you look at the page just quoted, one speaks of August 1994 at the top of the page, and there is -- and then again mid 1994, and you say "at that time." So it's really you should stop insisting in that case. I think your explanation, simply, it will not hold water. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that I understood the Trial Chamber to mean what I have shown, and that's how I gave evidence. Why would I be afraid to say that I was a member of the HDZ? I'm not. I, of course, didn't meddle with the transcript. And when I appeared here to give evidence, I was not an HDZ member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward, sir, your political party membership being whatever it was, you were a part of the top Herceg-Bosna HVO governmental/military leadership in 1992/1993, weren't you, the very top?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at that level, sir, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that you were more than just a political/military technocrat; you really were wearing a political hat as well as a military hat, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a political hat of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it the case in virtually every system that the more senior a military officer becomes, in terms of his position, and especially at the very top, there is an increasing political dimension or cross-over to the political and policy side; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be true, but I never went to -- into politics, nor did I ever have a political function until I came to the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not talking about, now, whether you were, again putting aside the HDZ political party at the moment. I'm talking about political at a broader level, the policy level. Give you another example, if I can hazard this as a hypothetical. In the United States, during Desert Storm, the first Desert Storm, the first Iraq operation, not the most current one, Colin Powell, commander of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, but at that point he was no longer acting as a soldier, technocrat, he was sitting at the political policy table, he was sitting across from President Bush and others and involved in those decisions, wasn't he? You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to object on technical reasons, we don't know that. There was some controversy between him and Cheney at the time, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly, that makes my point, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, as a soldier. As a soldier, he was the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, so obviously he's going to be talking to the Secretary of Defence. But I don't think that Mr. Scott should be in a position of testifying as to what was going on over there. Otherwise, he's personally injecting himself into the picture. These are not historical facts that are so notorious that you can just accept them as adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't want to get bogged down in this, Your Honour. It's not -- I don't want to use the time to debate it with Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The point is, sir, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that in many military situations, and I take it the same is true in Croatia, the closer you get to the top, the more political and policy-oriented your position becomes, doesn't it? You're no longer just talking about how many bullets the guy gets in the fox hole; you're talking about broad policy and political matters, strategy, budget requests, funding the army, political support for the military strategy? Isn't that true in virtually every military organisation, whether it's the United States, France, Switzerland, I dare say Hungary, and -- the United States and any of the others? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But why not mention Croatia. In 2000 and something, only due to the request of a number of generals for the supreme commander to receive them, he removed them all from their positions because he said, You have -- you shouldn't meddle with politics, you have nothing to do with politics. And 12 Croatian generals were -- simply had to retire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You want to talk about Croatia, let's talk about Croatia. You used -- you gave two examples in your testimony on the 11th of February. On the 11th of February, at transcript page 49296, on the one hand, you said that your first deputy, when you took one of your positions in the HVO -- excuse me, the Croatian Army: "My first deputy soon joined the Office of the President of the Republic, and there were also announcements that the commander would also leave and join the Ministry of Defence." People moved from the military side at those levels, they moved from the military side to the policy side, and that's -- look, there's nothing surprising or uncommon about that, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my deputy was a military official in the Office of the President of the Republic, because there is such a thing, and he monitors events in the army and nothing else. That's all his job. And my deputy was supposed to move to a position in the Ministry of Defence of Croatia, in which case he would have become a civilian, because at that time assistant ministers of defence were changing status from soldiers to civilian persons. And my deputy had a position in the president's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for cutting across the interpretation, but I do have to try to bring Mr. Petkovic's interventions sometimes to an end, and I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let's move forward with your exact involvement. You attended, in fact, both -- or the only two sessions of the HZ-HB Presidency between July 1992 and August 1993, where important decisions were made and laws were adopted, including in July 1992, for example, the Decree on the Armed Forces. You attended both of those important sessions of the Presidency, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you show me both so I can tell exactly which I attended?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can tell you, sir, I will if I have time, but you were at the 3 July 1992 meeting. You were there, you spoke there. You spoke about defence military matters. It was at that session that the Decree on Armed Forces was adopted. You were also present at the Presidency meeting on the 24th -- or the 28th, excuse me, of August, 1993, when the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was declared. And if we have time later, I'll show a video of that, and you'll see yourself in the video. These are two of the most important -- in fact, there were only about four or five in the entire history during this time, but these were the two most important meetings of the HZ-HB Presidency, and you were attended and acted in both of them, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended that meeting as a guest. My role was to inform everybody else, but otherwise I didn't have the right to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you certainly spoke at one of them, sir, and, again, we'll get there if we can, because it's in the record. You also attended sessions of the --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke about the military aspect, and that's why I was invited, to familiarise everybody with the military aspect. But I don't have the right to vote at these meetings. So I can only say what is required of me, and that is the military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Line 24 on page 76, it was translated, and now again the general said he didn't have the right to speak. I think it's a linguistical problem. He said he didn't have a right to vote. And it should be -- and that is why the next question was put. I guess it was misunderstanding between speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was certainly reacting to the English translation. If it was "did not have the right to vote," then I accept that, and that's not really my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were there, and you participated, sir, whether you voted or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I participated, and I informed those present about the military situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of Mr. Prlic's government, you attended at least -- at least five of those sessions, didn't you? On the 17th of April, 1993, on the 26th of May, 1993, the 31st of May, 1993, the 22nd of July, 1993, and the 9th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in October, too. Yes, those are all those sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as part of all this, one of the things you did was provide reports and information to the government - again, no surprise - about what was happening militarily and on defence matters, and you would give reports about that, didn't you -- wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to write biannual reports, and as part of the Defence Department's reports, they were sent to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look, as an example, at 2D -- in your binder, please, 2D01353 at the very -- toward the end of the binder, I believe, 2D01353. This is a report -- while you're finding that, sir, and to save a little bit of time, this is your report to the Defence Department, dated the 21st of September, 1992, and in the first paragraph you say: "Following a request of the HZ-HB government," that's Mr. Prlic's government, "for a report on the implementation of the priority duties and tasks regarding the establishment of the HVO Main Staff and the re-establishment," or "reorganisation" I believe might be a better translation, if I my be so bold, "of the existing units, we report as follows:" So this is an example, sir -- this is an example -- you were specifically requested by Mr. Prlic's government to report to it on military matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a report that I drafted at the request of the government, and I sent it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we go to 1D02423, 1D02423, this is a record of one of the meetings I mentioned to you a few moments ago, the 17th of April, 1993. The session was attended by, among others, Dr. J. Prlic, president, who chaired the session. We can also see Mr. Stojic there, and down toward the end of the line we see "Mr. Petkovic": "Agenda: Item 1. Discussion of the military and security situation in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." There's a report -- obviously a report given. This is April of 1993, a pretty critical time, April 1993. You were at that time the head of the Main Staff. And if I can draw your attention to the second-to-last paragraph of the document, in English page 2, first paragraph starting on that page; but, sir, in the Croatian version, if you find your way, please, to -- it's the next-to-last paragraph, obviously a report -- an assessment had been given, and it says this: "In accordance with these assessments, then, HZ-HB HVO adopted the position that the military organisation of the HVO and its Main Staff, along with the HZ-HB HVO Department of the Interior, should take all available measures in order to protect the Croatian population," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Several lines down: "The HZ-HB HVO requires the HVO Main Staff and the HZ-HB HVO to organise an effective defence and full protection," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. So in terms of some of things we've talked about this morning, this is an example, isn't it, where you go to a session of the government, you give a briefing, and the government makes decisions and gives you direction; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I've already said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I just want to make that, I suppose, very, very clear, sir. Will you go to P04 --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to add that the government won't contact me directly. It would go through its bodies that are responsible for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, when you were there on the 17th of April, you were there physically, apparently, according to this, and you were dealing directly and, I suppose, face to face with Bruno Stojic sitting there and Jadranko Prlic sitting there. So that seems pretty direct to me; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sitting in the area where all these present were. I provided them with information on the ABiH attack in the territory of Konjic, and this has to do with that area. It was my duty to brief the members of the government when I was invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course it was, of course it was. And if you can go, please, to P04343 sir, this is a -- just a very short document, but this is Mr. Nussbaum, who is the secretary of the HVO HZ-HB, the HVO government. And Mr. Nussbaum on in this case was sending a report of the minutes of a working meeting held on 18 August 1993 for your use to Zarko Tole. So isn't this another example of the government communicating directly with the military at the HVO Main Staff, communicating and sharing information back and forth, making reference to a working meeting on the 18th of August? That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. How else would you appear at a meeting? You can't just turn up. You have to be invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we're at the time of the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, had you occasions -- at least two occasion, perhaps more, but I know of at least two, you had occasions to actually attend meetings with President Tudjman in Croatia during 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember November 1993 in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you met with him once on the 24th of April in Croatia, again a pretty important time-period, and you also met with him on the 5th of November, 1993, just a few days after Stupni Do, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was invited to the meeting, and we went to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tudjman -- President Tudjman, he considered you, in fact, one of the leaders of Herceg-Bosna, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he couldn't have considered me as one of the leaders. I was the Chief of the Main Staff in Herceg-Bosna. As to who the leader in Herceg-Bosna was, that is well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I put to you that being the number-one military commander of almost anything makes you a pretty important leader, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an important role at the head of the army. As to how that should be compared with leaders outside the army, who occupy positions within the governmental hierarchy, well, that is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's go to slide 17, which is an excerpt of a presidential transcript on the 2nd of July, 1993, which is Exhibit P031112 [sic], page 54 of the transcript. President Tudjman talking: "Anyone else --"

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find it, please. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's on the screen, sir. You'll only see it on the screen and it will be translated to you. My apologies. If you want to turn to the transcript, it may or may not be in that binder. The full excerpt is on the slide. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. In the transcript, there is one "1" too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. 3112. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think if you want to look -- do you have it now, sir? If you want to look at it, you can, but everything I'm going to read to you is on the screen. The Usher's assistance, I'm sorry. Does he have it? I'm trying to assist you, sir. You'll have the Croatian transcript there in front of you. President Tudjman: "Anyone else? All right, gentlemen, let's finish. "With regard to sanctions, I do not think that in such a situation they pose a serious threat ... but we must be careful not to give them any direct cause to serve as an excuse for their policy. Clearly, we must not do this. But at the same time, we must take steps to protect Croatian interests in the territorial sense, too. And, you two, please, Minister Susak, General Bobetko, see about this and meet with Herceg-Bosna leaders there, with General Praljak, Petkovic, and Ambassador Sancevic, and their leaders there, with Boban and Prlic, to discuss exactly what should be done. But it goes without saying, do not lead the operation in such a way as to make it a direct involvement." I come back to you a question I put to you a moment ago, sir. President Tudjman considered you to be one of the leaders of Herceg-Bosna, didn't he? Praljak, Petkovic, Sancevic, Boban, Prlic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say "leader" anywhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, certainly in English it does, sir. And if it doesn't in Croatian, then you have me. But it says here: "You two, please, Minister Susak," the Defence Minister Susak, "General Bobetko," the head of the Croatian army, "see about this and meet with Herceg-Bosna leaders there," leaders there, "with General Praljak, Petkovic, and Ambassador Sancevic, and their leaders there, Boban and Prlic ..." He talks about leaders twice, doesn't he, including you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says with the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, and then there's a comma, and then it says -- or adds "with General Praljak and Petkovic," and then, "Ambassador Sancevic and their leaders there, with Boban and Prlic." So General Praljak and Petkovic aren't included in the category of leaders. There is a comma, after which you have the names "Praljak" and "Petkovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm happy to leave it with the Judges. Sir, you were also a member of the Bosnian Croat delegation at number of peace negotiations and conferences, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the Croatian delegation from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately how many times did you attend such conferences or sessions, just approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four conferences held in Geneva, and there were four meetings. The political aspect was dealt with in Geneva, or there were political meetings in Geneva, and military ones in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, sir, on this set of topics, you also frequently represented the HVO in front of the media, didn't you? You gave interviews, you had press conferences, and, in fact, you controlled the HVO's military's contact with the media, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I alone gave interviews for the media, but I didn't establish contact with the media, as you are saying. On occasion or from time to time, I would give interviews. So I only gave interviews for the media; I didn't establish contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you controlled access -- the media's access to the HVO, didn't you, at least the HVO military?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, "access to the HVO."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber can certainly stop and look at them, if they wish; but, for example, 2D00687 is an order that you issued on the 24th of November, 1993, prohibiting all HVO military contact with the media without your permission. Exhibit P00679, your order dated the 31st of October, 1992, right after Prozor, prohibiting contact with the media, or expressing -- forgive me, expressing your concern about the media, that "the coverage of some of these events were causing great problems for us in the foreign media," you were cognizant and paid attention to the media, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my duty. Not each and every commander or officer or HVO member should contact the media and give them statements of any kind. Information provided from the army, well, one knows who can provide such information, under what conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just make a brief correction. On the previous page, line 21, the year for the document is wrong. It should say "1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Counsel may be right, Your Honour, if I can just double-check.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is counsel referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I would be happy to help you. It is the wrong number, if you -- if you looked at the screen, this document has nothing to do with media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think, unfortunately, we're a document behind. The document -- counsel's correct. On 2D00687, it should be "1992." I misspoke, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But as you said just now, sir, and it's again nothing surprising, you can't just have everyone meeting and talking with the media willy-nilly, so to speak, and you controlled and you set a rule in place that there shouldn't be contact with the media without your permission; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that contact shouldn't be established with the media, because on item number 3 it is specified who can have contact with the media. Not just anyone can have the idea of contacting the media. And I think in all armies throughout the world, there are such provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in similar fashion, sir, you also controlled access or communications with the international organisations, didn't you; UNPROFOR, ECMM? Those communications could only take place with your approval? And again while you're thinking about that, I'll refer to P00797, again dated 24 November 1992, your order, sir: "There can be contacts with UNPROFOR and --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic -- one moment, please. General Petkovic, you have this document on the screen. You ban any contact with the media. This is in the three paragraphs, but in the reasoning you say that it is because individuals from the HVO have revealed military secrets. What did you mean by that? Is it because -- were you controlling the media by revealing military secrets?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we did not receive the interpretation of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to check. I'm going to ask the question again, sorry, because I didn't check. You see, usually when I ask a question, I look at the person I put the question to and don't look at the transcript. That's my mistake, because I'm not used to using the transcript, as such. So, General Petkovic, we have a document here in front of us. You say that you control -- or any contact with the media must have your prior approval. And this document shows that apparently the rationale is that there were individuals from the HVO who apparently revealed military secrets. What do you exactly refer to here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you know that information on the army -- on anyone's army is confidential, it's a military secret. There were commanders who spoke about all sorts of things because they weren't educated, they weren't well informed. They also provided information that did not fully correspond to the actual situation. They tried to emphasise their own importance and diminish the importance of others, and such a manner of communicating information is not permissible in any army. I then drafted an order, and I said if it is necessary for someone to establish contact with the media in a given area, then I will be the one to provide permission for that, because no one can simply decide on how to provide information to the media in any army. People simply didn't take into account the things that they were to speak about, the quantity of weapons, the situation in the army, et cetera, et cetera. Such matters are confidential, military secrets, and that is why we decided at all press conferences, and you can see this under item 3, we said that all press conferences would have to be permitted by the IPD, Defence Department. They knew how information should be provided to the media. You know, the press conferences are organised, and not each and every soldier can provide information or contact the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my pending question to you before was: You also controlled communications with UNPROFOR and the international organisations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have control over that. I had contact with UNPROFOR representatives, and at their request I would instruct my men as to how to establish contact with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well look, please, at P00797, which I began to refer to a few minutes ago, 24 November 1992, your order: "The commanders of the zones, staffs, and units can have contacts with UNPROFOR and the European Community members, as well as provide the latter with certain information, only with the permission of the chief of the HVO Main Staff"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That procedure had been a procedure that had been agreed on with UNPROFOR and other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The bottom line, sir, is that you played a very significant role in whatever information was provided to the media and whatever information was provided to the international organisations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contact with international organisations, at their request, and therefore I knew how I was to proceed, what I was to do. And you also don't allow anyone to write anything, so the army also has the right to protect itself and not to allow hundreds of people to provide information for the benefit of the media; therefore, yes, I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, throughout this time-period and what we've talked about in the last hour or so, coming full circle, what I put to you an hour, an half ago was: You were not some apolitical soldier, technocrat; you were a political policy actor as well, controlling access to the media, controlling access to international organisations, attending meetings of the government, attending meetings with President Tudjman, attending meetings of the HZ-HB Presidency; you were a major political actor; and, in fact, you felt often during this time more like a politician than a soldier, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't a politician. I was a soldier who, at given points in time, went to certain meetings, when invited. I wasn't a politician at the time, nor am I a politician now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look at -- this is a loose exhibit, not in the binders, a loose exhibit, P11167. And we can also put it up on Sanction, slide 18. This is from Exhibit P1167 [sic]. Sir, you gave an interview to "Glas Slavonije" on the 31st of December, 1994, and the very first paragraph, easy to find: "Major-General Milivoj Petkovic is remembered by many for his frequent television statements in the time of the fiercest conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, when he was Chief of Staff of the Croatian Defence Council. Asked whether he felt more like a soldier or like a politician in that time, he replied that it seemed to him that he was more politician than soldier ..." That's what you said in the interview on the 31st of December, 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does seem strange, the statement that I'm more politician than soldier. I really don't see myself as a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you may not, sir, but that's not what you said on this particular day. And I put it to you that given all your involvements that we spent the last hour and a half talking about, you were much more than a soldier, sir, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a general, sir, not a soldier, and I attended several meetings which were political in nature or of an international nature sometimes. And if we add all that up, apart from doing military business, I also participated in the -- in many meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, because of your high level of involvement in all these matters at both the military and the political level, the Tudjman government was very concerned when you were subpoenaed to testify in the Blaskic case, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how concerned they were. None of them ever told me that they were concerned. But they invited me and gave me the summons, and they also took some steps for me to give evidence under certain conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Oh, sir, I bet you anything that you knew they were concerned. I bet they told you how concerned they were, because in their own words, they thought, Petkovic is the man who knows too much, and for him to go to The Hague and testify raises all sorts of risk, because Petkovic knows too much. That was their concern, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they didn't say that to me. I don't know why they didn't. If they were concerned, they were obviously speaking about that among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's see. When you were summoned as a Court witness in the Blaskic case, you also received a set of questions or topics from the Court prior to your testimony, so you knew what questions were going to be asked; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the Tudjman government, or some of its representatives, helped you to prepare the right answers to those questions known in advance, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, they did not assist me in that. You could easily call up the questions that I got from the Trial Chamber, and I was the only one who knew the answers to those questions, and not the representatives of the Croatian government. It would be good if you could show me the questions that I received during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Receiving those questions or topics in advance, in fact, was a condition of the Croatian government allowing you to testify at this Tribunal, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And in the second instance, I also received the questions in advance, because the Trial Chamber thought that I needed some time to prepare. In the second instance, also, because the Croatian government was even less concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, our time is precious. You were accompanied and attended in your Blaskic testimony by an American lawyer named David Rifkin and a Croatian intelligence officer named Stefan Udiljak, weren't you? For the record, Udiljak, and my apologies if I've mispronounced it, U-d-i-l-j-a-k?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You obviously did, but you mis-positioned the American lawyer, because he represented the Croatian government, rather than General Petkovic. He obviously considered me a hostile witness, and he was another party to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure he considered you hostile, but he certainly did represent the Croatian government and I agree on that. But Mr. Udiljak was a member of the Croatian intelligence services, and it was Mr. Udiljak who contacted you about being a witness in the Blaskic case, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't contact me about being a witness in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Udiljak, sir, had become extensively involved by that time, in 1999, he had become extensively involved in matters concerning this Tribunal's efforts to locate and obtain the HVO archive, hadn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the HVO archive. I don't know anything about that. I left the HVO in 1994, and the archive stayed behind in the area where I was at the time. I have no idea where the archive was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was during the time, sir, and you know this, that the Tudjman government was concealing and keeping those archives from this Tribunal, wasn't it, and Mr. Udiljak was extensively involved in that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. As far as I know, there was an inquiry sent to Mr. Jelavic - that's what I learned from the media - who at the time was a minister of defence, or whatever he was. And the Federation of BiH and about the rest, I don't know. At the time, I served in Osijek, or maybe I was in Dubrovnik already. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, at this time -- and the Chamber has heard this name now several times, but you knew there was a man named Markica Rebic, who was the head of the Croatian intelligence service called SIS, and he was also the head of something called Operation -- or OA Haag, Operation Hague, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I learned about this for the first time from the newspapers.
