And about this Operation Hague, I heard for the first time here in this Tribunal, when there was a witness, but I have no knowledge about the Operation Hague. And as far as I know, in that document nobody has mentioned Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was the same Mr. Rebic who was also convicted by this Tribunal for contempt of court for disclosing protected witness information, wasn't he? In March 2006, this Tribunal issued a judgement of contempt against Mr. Rebic, and this was the man who was handling you in connection with your testimony in the Blaskic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Rebic never contacted me. The contacts in the Blaskic case were maintained by his Defence, and that's -- that applies to -- that's usual for any Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you and Mr. -- excuse me, strike that. Mr. Rebic and Mr. Bandic, who was a witness in this case in open session -- Mr. Rebic and Mr. Bandic were, in fact, conducting intelligence operations against this Tribunal, weren't they, trying to discover protected information, trying to develop sources inside the ICTY; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. You should have punished them if that's what you found out. It is hard to detect an intelligence man, especially in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to know, sir, that, in fact, Mr. Bandic at some point, because of his activities, was encouraged -- encouraged to leave the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is the same Mr. Bandic that you travelled with in Central Bosnia and the same Mr. Bandic who participated in the investigation concerning Stupni Do; correct? Your personal bodyguard, an intelligence operative, the man you travelled with repeatedly when you went to Central Bosnia, Mr. Bandic, and that's the man you put in charge of the Stupni Do investigation, one of your closest, most loyal lieutenants?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't say that. Especially when he was appointed to various diplomatic positions, I had no more contacts with him, and I didn't know what he was doing here in The Hague, whether he was with the Tribunal or with the embassy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I waited for Mr. Petkovic's answer. But I really would like a reference for what the Prosecutor is saying. This is the same Bandic who participated in the investigation concerning Stupni Do, I don't know the origin of that reference: For this, as far as I know, nobody has said anything like this in the courtroom before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. It's in one of the investigative reports by Mr. Bandic, and I would be happy to provide it. I can't give counsel the number at the moment, that Mr. Bandic was one of the persons who authored one of the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Bandic testified in this case, and he said that he was the one that whenever you travelled to Central Bosnia, he went with you. This is at 38245, 38246, 38259 to 60. One function was to be his bodyguard and then to actually conduct intelligence operations: "I was a member of the secret Counter-Intelligence Service, and this was part of my job. If we were going to Central Bosnia, very often it was only the two of us, Mr. Petkovic and I, and I drove." In any event, sir, let's turn to -- we only have a few minutes left, but at least hopefully we can start on this. Let's turn to Exhibit P08912 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we haven't said everything. Bandic's departure from Herceg-Bosna is also his departure from Petkovic. I never again had the opportunity to meet him again. So please don't link somebody's activities in one period to another period. We have nothing in common. He is not my superior, I am not his superior. We never co-operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, the Prosecutor is putting questions to you on the circumstances in which you testified in the Blaskic case. I have listened to you, and you said that you testified freely, without any problem whatsoever. Fine. On looking at your testimony in the Blaskic case, there was a problem at one point regarding the time. The Trial Chamber had taken some time and advised you of the fact that the hearing would resume on the following day, and that's when the problem arose. The Presiding Judge asks you for your opinion and asked you whether that would be a problem for you if the hearing were to resume on the following day, and this is what you said: "Your Honour --" This is in the French text, so page 22502: "Your Honour, when I was told last night that this would only last one day, my minister was informed and told me this: You may go there for one day." The answer you gave to the Presiding Judge seems to indicate that the minister of defence was following this very closely, since he said that you were only entitled to go there for one day. He's on a first-name basis with you. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I told you that the Croatian government tried to agree with the Tribunal, and finally did so, and was represented, among others, by a Mr. Udiljak, and I was told that these persons would interrupt me and were entitled to do so if a question were to be asked to me concerning the Republic of Croatia or anything about it, and I knew that. At the same time, the Croatian government, in communicating with the Tribunal, said that Petkovic would give evidence for an entire day in that trial, and it was accepted as such. However, many questions were still left, and the President of the Trial Chamber asked whether the evidence could be extended for another day. At that moment, Counsel Rifkin said, Well, I had received guarantees for one day, I have no guarantees for anything else. And then the President of the Trial Chamber addressed me, Mr. Petkovic, take my word for it, you have my guarantee. And I accepted that. So I stayed and gave evidence for as long as the Trial Chamber wanted. My evidence, as I said, had been agreed upon without anybody asking me anything about it. How the Croatian government was able to strike that agreement, I don't know. And it also got the right to be represented there by its lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before testifying, you were in contact with the Croatian minister of defence, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The Croatian minister of defence received a summons for my testimony, and I received the summons from the Ministry of Defence, because I didn't receive it personally. It was sent to the Croatian government, imposing an obligation on them to hand it to me. And the minister of defence invited me to come to see him, and I travelled from Dubrovnik to Zagreb. That's when I found out that Croatia would be represented by Mr. Rifkin and Mr. Udiljak. There was a conversation with the minister of about one hour, and they explained to me that they had the right to protect the interests of the Republic of Croatia and that they would intervene if a question were to be asked concerning the Republic of Croatia to which I didn't have the right to answer, because that was what the agreement was about. And I believe during my examination, there were two such interventions. Later on, everybody respected that and I was asked no more such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, when I put these questions to you about your testimony, I asked you whether your presence was subject to the approval of the Croatian authorities. Since the Trial Chamber had prepared a whole list of questions, and you stated what you had said, what I want to know is whether what you said had been "controlled," quote/unquote, by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, nobody controlled that testimony. I basically spoke about the military police and the authority over it. That was the central topic of my testimony, and there were also the special purpose units. The Croatian government didn't influence me in that respect. And, anyway, I knew the subject matter better than anybody else. And I testified to the best of my knowledge, and the President of the Trial Chamber said to me, General, you gave a brave statement, and he thanked me. The Croatian government displayed no interest whatsoever in the contents of my evidence. The minister of defence only spoke to me about Mr. Rifkin's representing the interests of Croatia during my testimony. That's the entire communication. And I can add that I asked the minister, at the end, whether I'm going there to testify in the Blaskic trial or in a trial where Croatia is being tried. So that was all my communication with one person only, and that was my then minister of defence. I believe his name was Mr. Miljavac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it's just about time to stop for today. There's one minute left. Would you like to put another question? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you very much. I'm about to start -- we would start another major document, and it would be better if we start tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, as you all know, we will be sitting tomorrow in the afternoon. We will have only one break tomorrow afternoon. I wish you all a good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
